chapters.title: Chapter 4: Income That Does Not Follow the Slabs

lessons.title: Combining Slab Income and Special Rate Income in One Computation

body.text: Special-rate income never pushes your salary into a higher slab. But it does count towards Total Income, so it can cost you the ₹12 lakh rebate or drag your whole tax bill into surcharge.

children.text: Most real taxpayers have both kinds of income: a salary taxed through the slabs, and some equity gains, crypto profits or a quiz show prize taxed at fixed rates. The law handles this by running two tracks side by side and then merging them for the final adjustments. Once you see the two tracks, the interactions that surprise people become predictable.
The Two-Track Computation
Compute Total Income, including all special-rate income.
This single figure is used for the rebate test and the surcharge thresholds.
Split it into slab-rate income and each type of special-rate income.
If slab-rate income is below the nil slab, use the shortfall against eligible capital gains, as covered in the last lesson.
Track A: apply the slabs to slab-rate income only.
The slabs start from zero for this portion, whatever the size of your special-rate income.
Track B: apply each special rate to its own income.
20% on short-term listed equity gains, 12.5% on long-term gains above any exemption, 30% on winnings and crypto.
Merge: add both tracks, then apply the rebate, surcharge, marginal relief and cess.
Under the new regime the rebate can only cancel Track A tax. Surcharge on Track B tax from equity gains and dividends is capped at 15%.

body.caption: Rebate and surcharge eligibility are both decided by Total Income, which includes Track B income

children.text: Interaction 1: No Slab Push-Up

A common fear is that selling shares "puts me in a higher bracket". It does not. If your slab-rate income is ₹18 lakh, Track A tax is ₹1,60,000 whether you have zero gains or ₹40 lakh of gains. The gains are taxed separately at their own rate. This is different from slab-rate extras like FD interest, rent or short-term gains on gold, which are added to your salary and do climb the same staircase.
Interaction 2: Losing the Rebate Because of Gains

Aarti, a resident bank officer in Vadodara on the new regime, has ₹11,00,000 of salary income after the standard deduction. The only question is how much short-term equity gain she books in tax year 2026-27.

body.title: Aarti: ₹1 Lakh vs ₹2 Lakh of Short-Term Equity Gains

columns.label: ₹1,00,000 of Gains
points: Total Income: ₹12,00,000, within the rebate limit
Track B: 20% of ₹1,00,000 = ₹20,000, not covered by the rebate

columns.label: ₹2,00,000 of Gains
points: Total Income: ₹13,00,000, above the rebate limit
No rebate; the excess over ₹12 lakh (₹1,00,000) exceeds the tax, so no marginal relief either

body.text: Only ₹20,800 of that ₹72,800 is tax on the extra gain itself. The other ₹52,000 is her salary tax, which the rebate had been cancelling. For anyone with salary income between roughly ₹8 lakh and ₹12 lakh, the timing and size of capital gains can matter more than the gains tax rate.

children.text: Interaction 3: Gains That Trigger Surcharge on Your Salary Tax

Sameer is a consulting partner in Gurugram on the new regime. His slab-rate income is ₹46,00,000, just below the ₹50 lakh surcharge threshold. In tax year 2026-27 he also sells a mutual fund portfolio he has held for nine years, booking ₹21,25,000 of long-term equity gains.

body.caption: Sameer's Tax, New Regime, Total Income ₹67,25,000

cells: 10%, as Total Income exceeds ₹50 lakh; the 15% cap on gains is not binding
Not applicable, income far above the relief zone

body.title: What Sameer's ₹21.25 Lakh of Gains Really Cost

children.text: Without the gains, Sameer's tax would have been ₹9,98,400. With them it is ₹13,84,240, an increase of ₹3,85,840. Almost ₹1 lakh of that increase is surcharge on his salary tax, which his salary alone would never have attracted. Spreading the sale across two tax years, or across family members who genuinely own the units, could have kept his Total Income below ₹50 lakh.

body.label: What Special-Rate Income Does and Does Not Affect
body.value: Affects: rebate test, surcharge rate. Does not affect: your slab rates
body.context: Track A tax is computed as if special-rate income did not exist. Every threshold based on Total Income sees all of it.

body.title: Going deeper: the 15% surcharge cap at ₹3 crore

children.text: Rakesh, a Surat textile promoter on the new regime, has ₹1,00,00,000 of slab-rate income and sells shares with ₹2,01,25,000 of long-term gains. Total Income is ₹3,01,25,000, so the surcharge rate is 25%. Track A tax is ₹25,80,000 and Track B tax is 12.5% of ₹2,00,00,000 = ₹25,00,000. Surcharge is 25% on the slab tax (₹6,45,000) but only 15% on the gains tax (₹3,75,000), a total of ₹10,20,000. With cess, tax payable is ₹63,44,000. Without the 15% cap, surcharge would have been ₹12,70,000 and he would have paid ₹2,60,000 more.

body.title: Before You Sell: A Mixed-Income Tax Check
steps: Estimate your slab-rate income for the tax year: salary after standard deduction, interest, rent and any slab-rate gains
Add the special-rate income you plan to book to get projected Total Income
If slab-rate income alone is at or below ₹12 lakh, check whether the gains push Total Income above ₹12 lakh and cost you the rebate
If Total Income will be near ₹50 lakh, ₹1 crore or ₹2 crore, check whether the gains trigger a higher surcharge on your whole tax
If either threshold is crossed, consider spreading the sale across tax years, or holding short-term positions past 12 months so they become long-term
Remember the rebate never covers Track B tax, so budget for tax on special-rate income even if your salary tax is zero

children.text: Practice

body.title: Salary Plus Short-Term Gains
body.prompt: Bhavna, a resident in Mysuru on the new regime, has ₹9,00,000 of salary income after the standard deduction and ₹2,00,000 of short-term gains on listed shares. What is her total tax payable, including cess?
body.explanation: Total Income is ₹11,00,000, within the ₹12 lakh limit. Track A slab tax on ₹9,00,000 is ₹20,000 + 10% of ₹1,00,000 = ₹30,000, fully cancelled by the rebate. Track B tax is 20% of ₹2,00,000 = ₹40,000, which the rebate cannot touch. With 4% cess: ₹41,600.

body.title: Do Gains Raise the Slab Rate?
body.question: Gaurav has ₹18,00,000 of salary income after the standard deduction. In the same year he books ₹30,00,000 of long-term gains on listed shares. Which statement is correct under the new regime?
options: His salary is now taxed at 30% because Total Income crosses ₹24 lakh
His salary slab tax stays ₹1,60,000, and the gains are taxed separately at 12.5% above ₹1,25,000
His gains are taxed at his 20% slab rate
Total Income of ₹48 lakh triggers 10% surcharge on all his tax
body.explanation: Special-rate income does not push slab-rate income into higher slabs. Track A tax on ₹18 lakh is ₹1,60,000 regardless of the gains. Track B tax is 12.5% of ₹28,75,000 = ₹3,59,375. Total Income is ₹48 lakh, which is below the ₹50 lakh surcharge threshold, so option D is also wrong.

body.title: What Total Income Decides
body.textWithBlank: Special-rate income does not change your slab rates, but it counts towards Total Income for the rebate test and the ___ thresholds.
body.explanation: Both the ₹12 lakh rebate limit and the ₹50 lakh, ₹1 crore, ₹2 crore and ₹5 crore surcharge thresholds are tested against Total Income, which includes every rupee of special-rate income.

body.title: Karthika's March Sale
body.scenario: Karthika, a resident government school teacher in Madurai on the new regime, has ₹11,00,000 of salary income after the standard deduction every year. In March 2027 she wants to sell shares bought in November 2026, booking ₹2,00,000 of short-term gains, to fund a family wedding in May 2027. She expects the same salary next year.
body.prompt: What will the sale cost her in tax if she sells everything in March 2027? Suggest a better plan and quantify the saving.
body.modelAnswer: Selling everything in March 2027 puts Total Income for tax year 2026-27 at ₹13,00,000. She loses the rebate on her ₹50,000 of slab tax and pays 20% on the ₹2,00,000 of gains: ₹90,000 plus cess, or ₹93,600. Better plan: sell half in March 2027 and half in April 2027, which falls in tax year 2027-28. Each year her Total Income is exactly ₹12,00,000, so the rebate cancels her slab tax and she pays only 20% on ₹1,00,000 of gains plus cess: ₹20,800 a year, ₹41,600 in total. That saves ₹52,000. An even better option, if the wedding date allows, is to hold the shares until after November 2027 so the gains become long-term. Then the first ₹1,25,000 is exempt and the rest is taxed at 12.5%. This assumes her salary and the tax rules stay the same next year.

points: Tax is computed on two tracks: slab rates on slab-rate income, fixed rates on each type of special-rate income
Special-rate income never pushes slab-rate income into a higher slab
Total Income, including special-rate income, decides whether you get the rebate and which surcharge rate applies
Under the new regime the rebate cancels only slab tax, never tax on special-rate income
Gains that take Total Income past ₹12 lakh can cost you the entire rebate on your salary tax
Gains that take Total Income past a surcharge threshold add surcharge to your salary tax too, though surcharge on equity gains tax is capped at 15%
Timing sales across tax years, or letting short-term holdings turn long-term, can save far more than the headline gains tax rate suggests

body.text: Examples assume resident individuals under the new regime for tax year 2026-27 and that tax rules stay unchanged across years. Marginal relief calculations with mixed income can be more complex than shown. This lesson is for education only and is not tax or investment advice.
